newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE-Welcome to Miami, "the unreal city".
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Welcome to Miami, "the unreal city".

text.p: From the mock colonial mansions of Coral Gables to the dolphin steaks on restaurant menus, you often get the feeling nothing in Miami is quite real.

It could be because most people in this U.S. city speak Spanish and the downtown streets throb to a salsa beat -- or because a tropical town, where most people experience ice only in cocktails, has one of the highest-flying teams in the National Hockey League, the Florida Panthers.

Day in and day out, politicians and personalities, crooks and cops insist on behaving as though they were playing roles in a B-movie or a television serial. "You tell people you're from Miami and they duck," said writer Carl Hiaasen, who writes about the beautiful, the bad and the bizarre in a newspaper column and a series of funny novels.
Raw material litters the ground. These stories are true:
-- This summer, U.S. Attorney Kendall Coffey resigned following allegations he bit a dancer while enjoying himself in a strip joint.

-- A bogus doctor with credentials from Nicaragua performed plastic surgery on dozens of women. After maiming one of them, Henry Castillo was nabbed last month when he offered undercover detectives a special deal on liposuction.

-- Dressing in pastel suits like Don Johnson in "Miami Vice" was not enough for Abram Zayas. In an effort to attract women, he walked around in full police uniform and even helped to investigate crimes before police caught on.
It's a tough town and crime is rife so citizens are understandably blase at times.
Richard Lopez was feeding ducks on a canal when a box floated by. Hauling it in, he found the mutilated remains of a woman. He told police he was disappointed it was not money.

"One of the wondrous things about Florida, Rudy Graveline thought as he chewed on a jumbo shrimp, was the climate of unabashed corruption. There was absolutely no trouble from which money could not extradite you," Hiaasen wrote in "Skin Tight" about Graveline, an incompetent plastic surgeon.
It remains to be seen if Miami's former city manager and an elected commissioner, indicted in September on corruption and bribery charges, can wriggle out of their predicament.

In true Elmore Leonard style, Commissioner Miller Dawkins allegedly took delivery of a bag stuffed with dirty money in a family restaurant on the Dixie Highway, according to the indictment. His accomplice was wired for sound by the FBI. He has pleaded guilty and awaits sentencing.
One reason for former City Manager Cesar Odio's alleged avarice, authorities said, is that he wanted to buy a Rolex watch. Odio denies the charges. His trial is set for January.
The Magic City, as tourist officials like to call it, is also a city of contrasts.

Ocean Drive on Miami Beach is a prime preening ground for trendy young Americans, where astoundingly beautiful models -- women and men -- stroll past sidewalk cafes dressed in next to nothing and even the police have gel in their hair.
A few streets behind, an army of old folk trying to enjoy a retirement in the sun shuffle along on walking sticks or peer out from behind the curtains of old apartment buildings.

Crime-plagued, dilapidated Liberty City is a poor black ghetto where the American Dream has failed miserably, while in Coral Gables millionaires from Colombia and Cuba live in mansions built by Henry George Merrick, who went bankrupt in the 1920s before he could complete his dream of building a Mediterranean city.

"Things are very comfortable for many people. The children of the exiles aren't going to go back and fight Castro. They're having a good time here," said one Cuban-American businessman taking lunch in the Little Havana neighbourhood.

The Cuban American community is united in its loathing for President Fidel Castro, whose name hangs over Miami like a ghost at a banquet. But they still end up fighting among themselves in the name of freedom and democracy.

Right-wing groups firebomb restaurants and hound foreign singers out of town if they fail to denounce "the bearded one" in strong enough terms. Men in paramilitary uniforms turn up at demonstrations hurling vitriol at anyone who talks of rapprochement with the Cuban leader.

Decades of political turmoil in Latin America is reflected in Miami's ethnic mix, which includes many Haitians, Nicaraguans and Dominicans as well as Cubans. "The Cubans hate the Colombians, the Colombians hate the Salvadoreans, who hate the Peruvians, and everyone hates the poor old Haitians," was the view of one female lawyer as she sipped wine in the Biltmore Hotel, grandly modelled on Sevilla's Giralda Tower.
"Anglo" housewives, as non-Hispanic whites are called, complain the Latins are responsible for the appalling driving on city roads.

If anyone is having the last laugh, it is probably the Native Americans, who have seen everyone from Spanish conquistadores to British redcoats come and go. They are raking in money in bingo casinos on their reservations, which are exempt from state gambling laws.
"Seminole Bingo" is a must for many blue-haired ladies -- a minibus will pick them up from their homes and run them up to the reservation for a night of gaming.
Only in Miami.
